Disclaimer: I don’t think I’ve ever written a book review, even in school, so I’ll do my best.

 

First, a shout-out to @Shekelstein6M for the recommendation. Within a day or two of reading his comment, I downloaded the book and started it. Thank you, really.

So, No More Mr Nice Guy!: A Proven Plan for Getting What You Want In Love, Sex and Life, is a kind of self-help book (is that what they are still called?), by Dr Robert Glover. The author is a therapist specialising in the “Nice Guy Syndrome”, to help “nice guys” to recover from the syndrome and start getting what they need and want in life.

This help is more targeted for men, though it can easily be read by women who want to understand more their “nice guy” partners and/or want to support them in their recovery.

The book itself, I “read” as an audiobook, mostly on walks and in the car. It was close to seven hours’ long, but with the way Dr Glover narrates (he narrates his own book), I found that it was comfortable enough to listen at a speed of 1.25x. This means, with some rewinding, it took me about six hours to listen. I consumed the book over three days, as it can get a little heavy and emotional, so I found I needed some time to process it and to have a break.

This might be an obvious thing to say, but No More Mr Nice Guy! can be treated in two ways: either as a full, dedicated recovery programme or less seriously, kind of letting its ideas wash over you and take what you want out of it.

For those who would like to follow-through with a long-term recovery programme, a “recovering nice guy” (as Dr Glover calls those men seeking help to recover from the “Nice Guy Syndrome), the book contains activities, called “Breaking Free activities”, of which there are nearly 50. Since I was reading this mostly outside of the home, I only did a few of the activities, but I found they were very useful in allowing me to reflect seriously on my situations.

The first chapter, describing the Nice Guy Syndrome, was eerily accurate for me (and as the book goes on, other men state too). What I found very helpful was that Dr Glover gave a tonne of examples of men he has treated, to cover the wide-range of “nice guys”. When I say the wide-range, it means how their symptoms are manifested and how they became “nice guys”.

What I can say is that the author hooks you in straight away with his professionalism: you can tell he has a wealth of experience in this subject. For me, it meant I couldn’t wait to hear more about “myself” and how Dr Glover could help.

As mentioned above, it took me a few sessions to listen to this book, and I see now that I did so more-or-less in conjunction with how the author split-up the book.

The first part is him describing the “Nice Guy Syndrome” and how it came about (it’s mostly how in childhood your needs were not met in timely and judicious manner). It also alludes to how he can help. Dr Glover kind of lays it on thick he and really demotivates you, breaks you down, which I think is intentional, to build you back up. Honestly, I had to stop towards the end of the section, because I was getting emotional.

The second part of the book is more about a self-reflection on the advice Dr Glover gives about reclaiming your masculinity and personal power and making your needs a priority. This builds upon the first part of the book in the sense it is still focusing on the inner-you, but you can see the progression to tangible changes needed.

The third part of the book is just that, making real changes in your life, with the focus on three areas of your life: love; sex and; life (including career). With the knowledge of who you are and Dr Glover’s wisdom in the first two-thirds of the book, it makes sense to make these changes in your life that he suggests.

Throughout the book, Dr Glover refers back to the men in the first chapter (and more, I think), so the reader can feel connected to real-live men; the author uses situations in his own life as examples too. I did feel comforted realising that there really were men with my issues and my feelings out in the world.

What did I get out of the book. I think the biggest take-away for me was to stop acting like a victim, that it’s okay to ask for help. On more practical matters, one action with which I’ll follow-up is starting to be closer to men (most “nice guys” have women friends, finding it uncomfortable to interact with men on a deeper level).

Dr Glover did talk about, more at the beginning of the book, about how it wasn’t just the childhoods of “nice guys” that robbed them of their masculinity, but the liberated era after WWII. He did go over that again towards the end, but I would’ve like to have seen that explored a bit deeper.

So, I fell into the second category where I’ve taken what I can out of this book, rather than going through full recovery. I feel that this is because of my mentality of being open to different points-of-view and thinking, and I really do think that most Voaters, by their nature, will be in my boat too. It’s not to say that I’ve just changed overnight, I will be working on myself as ever, with advice from No More Mr Nice Guy! in the front of my mind.

I highly recommend reading this book, and more so, as an audiobook. If one wants to supplement the audio with the paperback, I can see how that would help with focusing on improving oneself in the long-term as per the advice contained in the book.
